q: How do alloys generally compare with the pure metals they are made from?
options: They are always softer and weaker
They are better electrical conductors
They are often harder and stronger
They always have lower melting points
explain: Mixing in other atoms usually makes the metal harder and stronger, so alloys are often more useful.

q: Which description of a structure represents an alloy?
options: A lattice of identical atoms in regular layers
A lattice with atoms of two different sizes mixed together
A lattice of alternating positive and negative ions
Separate small molecules held by weak forces
explain: An alloy contains atoms of different sizes, which disturbs the regular layers of a pure metal.

q: Which description of a structure represents a pure metal?
options: Atoms of two different sizes mixed together
Identical atoms arranged in regular layers
Positive and negative ions alternating in a lattice
Small molecules arranged in a lattice
explain: A pure metal has only one type of atom, so the layers are regular.

q: Why are alloys often harder than the pure metals in them?
options: Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding over each other easily
Alloys have stronger metallic bonds because they contain more electrons
All the atoms are the same size so the layers lock together
Alloys contain covalent bonds between the metals
explain: The different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over one another as easily.

q: Why is a pure metal usually soft and malleable?
options: The atoms are held by weak covalent bonds
The positive ions are free to move out of the lattice
The layers of identical atoms can slide over each other
The metal contains many different sizes of atom
explain: In a pure metal the regular layers slide when a force is applied, so the metal changes shape without breaking.

q: Which of these is an alloy?
options: Copper(II) oxide
Zinc
Cryolite
Brass
explain: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc; zinc is an element and the other two are compounds.

q: Which row correctly describes an alloy?
options: Brass | copper and tin | harder than copper
Stainless steel | iron and chromium | resists rusting
Stainless steel | iron and copper | resists rusting
Brass | iron and zinc | harder than copper
explain: Stainless steel contains iron with chromium and other elements and does not rust easily, while brass is copper and zinc.

q: Pure iron is soft, but steel is hard. Why does adding a little carbon make the iron harder?
options: Carbon atoms make the iron atoms smaller so they fit together better
Carbon forms ionic bonds with iron
Carbon atoms add delocalised electrons that stop the layers moving
Carbon atoms are a different size so the layers of iron atoms cannot slide easily
explain: The carbon atoms differ in size from iron atoms, distorting the layers and making sliding more difficult.

q: Steel is stronger than pure iron. What is steel?
options: Iron mixed with a small amount of carbon
A compound of iron and carbon only
Pure iron with a layer of rust
Iron mixed with a large amount of zinc
explain: Steel is an alloy, a mixture of iron with a small percentage of carbon.

q: Why is mild steel not suitable for making cutlery?
options: It is too hard to shape
It conducts electricity
It rusts in contact with water and air
It has too low a density
explain: Mild steel is mostly iron and rusts, whereas stainless steel resists rusting.

q: Which change would make a pure metal harder?
options: Heating the metal
Removing the delocalised electrons
Adding atoms of a different size
Making the layers more regular
explain: Different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding, which is how alloys are made harder.

q: A 200 g sample of brass contains 130 g of copper, and the rest is zinc. What is the percentage of zinc by mass?
explain: Zinc = 200 − 130 = 70 g, so the percentage is 70 ÷ 200 × 100 = 35%.

q: Which list shows metals in order of decreasing reactivity, most reactive first?
options: Calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron
Calcium, zinc, magnesium, iron
Magnesium, calcium, iron, zinc
Iron, zinc, magnesium, calcium
explain: The reactivity series runs … calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper …

q: Which pair of non-metals is included in the reactivity series?
options: Oxygen and nitrogen
Chlorine and iodine
Sulfur and silicon
Carbon and hydrogen
explain: Carbon and hydrogen are placed in the series as reference points, for extraction and for reaction with acids.

q: Which statement describes sodium added to cold water?
options: It melts, moves on the surface and fizzes
It sinks and reacts slowly
It floats and does not react
It burns with a bright white flame
explain: Sodium reacts vigorously with water, producing hydrogen; the heat melts the metal, which floats and moves around.

q: Which equation correctly represents calcium reacting with cold water?
options: Ca(s) + H₂O(l) → CaO(s) + H₂(g)
Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + O₂(g)
Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Ca(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)
explain: Calcium and cold water give calcium hydroxide and hydrogen, and the equation is balanced with 2H₂O.

q: Which equation correctly represents magnesium reacting with steam?
options: Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + O₂(g)
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgH₂(s) + O₂(g)
2Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → Mg₂O(s) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g)
explain: Magnesium reacts with steam to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen; magnesium oxide is MgO.

q: Which metal does not produce bubbles of hydrogen when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Zinc
Copper
Iron
Magnesium
explain: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.

q: Equal pieces of magnesium, zinc and iron are added to separate samples of the same dilute hydrochloric acid. In which order do they bubble, fastest to slowest?
options: Magnesium, iron, zinc
Magnesium, zinc, iron
Zinc, magnesium, iron
Iron, zinc, magnesium
explain: The more reactive the metal, the faster the reaction, and the order of reactivity is magnesium, zinc, iron.

q: Metal W reacts with cold water. Metal X does not react with cold water but reacts with steam. Metal Y does not react with steam but reacts with dilute acid. Metal Z does not react with dilute acid. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
options: X, W, Y, Z
W, Y, X, Z
Z, Y, X, W
W, X, Y, Z
explain: A metal that reacts with cold water is more reactive than one needing steam, then one reacting only with acid, then one with no reaction.

q: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P gives many bubbles very quickly, Q gives a few bubbles slowly, R gives no bubbles and S gives a moderate stream of bubbles. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
options: P, S, Q, R
P, Q, S, R
R, Q, S, P
S, P, Q, R
explain: More vigorous bubbling means a more reactive metal and no reaction means the least reactive.

q: Which of these metals is above hydrogen in the reactivity series?
options: Copper
Silver
Iron
Gold
explain: Iron is above hydrogen and displaces it from acids, while copper, silver and gold are below it.

q: Where is carbon placed in the reactivity series?
options: Between magnesium and aluminium
Between iron and hydrogen
Between aluminium and zinc
Between copper and silver
explain: Carbon sits between aluminium and zinc, so it can reduce oxides of zinc and iron but not aluminium oxide.

q: Magnesium is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which observation is correct?
options: The solution turns darker blue and the magnesium dissolves
The solution stays blue and bubbles of hydrogen form
The blue solution turns green and a grey solid forms
The blue colour fades and a brown solid forms
explain: Magnesium displaces copper, which forms as a brown solid, and the blue Cu²⁺ ions are used up.

q: Which mixture will produce no reaction?
options: Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution
Copper added to zinc sulfate solution
Magnesium added to iron(II) sulfate solution
Iron added to silver nitrate solution
explain: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from solution.

q: Which ionic equation shows zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate solution?
options: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s)
Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn⁺(aq) + Cu(s)
Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn(s) + Cu(s)
explain: Zinc atoms lose two electrons to form Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions gain them to form copper, and the charges balance.

q: Zinc displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution. What explains this?
options: Zinc atoms gain electrons more easily than copper atoms
Zinc is a better conductor of electricity
Zinc atoms lose electrons more easily than copper atoms
Copper ions are less dense than zinc ions
explain: The more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form positive ions by losing electrons.

q: Iron is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which statement about the redox change is correct?
options: Iron atoms lose electrons and are oxidised
Iron atoms gain electrons and are reduced
Copper ions lose electrons and are oxidised
Sulfate ions gain electrons and are reduced
explain: Iron forms Fe²⁺ by losing electrons, which is oxidation, and the Cu²⁺ ions gain them and are reduced.

q: Aluminium is above zinc in the reactivity series but reacts very little with dilute acid at first. Why?
options: Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
A thin layer of aluminium oxide protects the metal
Aluminium is a non-metal
Aluminium forms an insoluble hydroxide with the acid
explain: The unreactive oxide layer covers the surface and stops the acid reaching the aluminium underneath.

q: A piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. There is no fizzing at first, but after some time it fizzes vigorously. Why?
options: The acid slowly makes the foil more reactive
The foil warms and changes into a non-metal
Hydrogen first has to be added to the acid
The acid slowly removes the oxide layer
explain: Once the aluminium oxide layer has been dissolved by the acid, the reactive aluminium beneath reacts and gives hydrogen.
